Decades after Neil Armstrong’s bootprint, the Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter flew low over the Sea of Tranquility, Hadley Rille, Taurus-Littrow and the other Apollo sites. From 20–50 kilometers up, its cameras resolved the lunar module descent stages, the dark trails of rover tracks, the glint of experiment packages, and even the shadows of flags.

The same details appear at every other landing site.

The pictures were taken by a camera built and operated at Arizona State University. Japan’s Kaguya, India’s Chandrayaan-2 and South Korea’s Danuri independently imaged the same hardware. Lasers fired from Earth still bounce off the retroreflectors the crews left behind. The rocks they brought home have been studied in laboratories around the world.

The past 3 yrs have been the hardest of my professional life. I'm both proud to have survived so far and embarrassed that I got myself into this situation in the first place. 

I purchased in 2023 via SBA 7a, underwritten as a $3M rev business. QofE and my own diligence missed two main things: the seller's second business was floating most cashflow issues and their local reputation was unusable. I rebranded to "Cooper" within 95 days on Jan 1, 2024.

This industry runs on relationships and reputation. I instantly became an unknown entity and revenue dropped 95% overnight compared to what was underwritten. There are a lot of stories to tell about 2024, but tl;dr I scratched and clawed back to only $1.7M rev by the end of the year. I emptied my savings and depended on hard money to survive.

Throughout that year, I made fundamental changes to our sales and operations. We focused on municipal work because I could personally handle the administrative burden and the playing field felt more fair. But our bid -> sale -> collection timeline ballooned to around 9-12 months. Changes wouldn't bear fruit for a long time. 

In Q2 2025, our 2024 efforts started to take effect. By EOY, we had grown to $3.65M in rev while improving gross margins. However, we were completely cash poor due to growth capital needs and crazy interest payments. We leaned on MCAs to get through because we couldn't compromise all our new client relationships.

This year, we professionalized further, increasing both sales and GM. Our annualized revenue is ~$6m and this will be the first year with substantial EBITDA ($1.2M). We took some less horrible debt and I'm working on a larger refi to stabilize a bit. I am still just trying to maintain overall debt coverage.

All this time, I haven't paid myself a cent. My team has remained underpaid. Everything has depended on selling the vision to both employees and clients. Selling the future to fund the present. 

As I reflect on the last 3 years, I feel optimistic about the future. I am a MUCH better operator than in 2023. My team is lean and loyal. And any further growth should be upside I can capture. 

But if you asked if it was all worth it, I'm not sure how I'd respond. For the past 3 yrs, I've chronically felt nauseous about paying bills, payroll, potential liability/conflict in our work. I've been less present at home. I've been very boring with friends. My health has taken a backseat to the needs of the business. Not to mention my net worth has tanked compared to pre-purchase levels. 

Our conservative plan is to hit $8M in '27, $12M in '28, then $19M in '29. I know it will continue to be hard, but I'm excited to outgrow the first phase of ownership and work on a fresh set of challenges. 

Here's to the next three years.

Imagine a computer that took so long to boot, the mean time to failure (MTTF) was…shorter than the boot time!

ASCI Q, the supercomputer, failed every 6.5 hours from 2002-2003. 

It also, worryingly, took as much as ~8 hours for a whole-machine reboot!

Kind of a problem when the Top 2 supercomputer in the world has a utilization of only ~60%! Supposedly, they had a a “few good weeks” exceeding 85%…but that was rare.

Now, it wasn’t really their fault. A suspicion was raised that cosmic rays could be causing uncorrectable bit flips. To test, you’d need to essentially simulate the sun on an accelerated timescale.

…which, isn’t a problem when you’re at Los Alamos. They pointed their own neutron beam at ASCI Q; just 5 seconds of beam time equaled 6+ years of normal Sun exposure!

It narrowed down to the lack of correctable parity in the L2 Cache of their Alpha CPUs. Obviously, it’s since been figured out, (ASCI Q was *very* experimental at the time) with future machines using ECC protected L2 as well as better software fallbacks + checkpointing.

Sometimes you have to deal with really, really unreliable systems when you’re pushing the frontier!

Elon rightfully highlights the word "bed" in his original posting. 

Raising the head of your bed is not the same as using a taller pillow.

A tall pillow raises the head relative to the chest and can push the neck into forward flexion.

That can mean:

- a more collapsible upper airway
- greater resistance to airflow
- altered cervical alignment
- much higher pressure on the back of the neck

Experimental airway measurements found that forward flexion made the passive upper airway easier to collapse, while extending the head shifted it strongly in the opposite direction. Awake human testing also found higher airway resistance with the neck flexed forward.

Higher pillow heights have separately been shown to change cervical alignment and substantially increase pressure around the head and neck.

Raising the head end of the whole bed is mechanically different.

The head, shoulders, torso and hips stay on one continuous incline. The elevation comes from changing the angle of the body rather than creating it by bending the neck forward.

Human studies of head-of-bed elevation in people with obstructive sleep apnea have found:
- fewer apnea and hypopnea events
- higher minimum overnight oxygen saturation
- particularly large reductions in breathing events while sleeping on the back

In one 2017 study using a 7.5° elevation, apnea and hypopnea events fell by roughly one-third.

The evidence therefore points toward separating the two jobs:

- the bed creates the incline
- the pillow supports the neck
- the neck stays close to neutral
- for side sleeping, pillow height follows shoulder-to-neck distance rather than one universal height
- in some back sleepers, turning the head somewhat to the side may further reduce airway narrowing

Whole-body elevation preserves a much more neutral head-neck relationship while still providing the positional effect of sleeping on an incline.

For diagnosed or suspected sleep apnea, these positional changes are adjuncts, not replacements for proper assessment or prescribed treatment.

This is general information, not medical advice, and doesn't replace talking to a doctor or other qualified physician, especially with an existing health condition.

References

Choi JK et al. (2000). Effect of jaw and head position on airway resistance in obstructive sleep apnea.

Kim HC et al. (2015). The Effect of Different Pillow Heights on the Parameters of Cervicothoracic Spine Segments.

Ren S et al. (2016). Effect of pillow height on the biomechanics of the head-neck complex: investigation of the cranio-cervical pressure and cervical spine alignment.

//The Wire//1300Z September 28, 2026//
//PRIORITY//
//BLUF: INCIDENT REPORTED AT RAF FAIRFORD AS MULTIPLE MEN ARRESTED IN MULTIPLE VEHICLES NEAR THE AIRBASE PERIMETER.//
-----BEGIN TEARLINE-----
-International Events-

United Kingdom: Yesterday a possible terror attack was foiled at Fairford Airbase, after a group of men were discovered acting suspiciously in the vicinity of the base. Local authorities state that a local farmer visually observed three vans parked in the roadway just outside the base. When the farmer approached the vehicles blocking the road, a group of masked men fled from the scene. After the alarm was raised, authorities responded and a total of five men were detained after being found hiding in the woods near the van site. A search of their vans revealed large containers of hazardous material, which prompted a mass evacuation of the local area. A total of 85x homes were evacuated for several hours while EOD personnel examined the contents of the vans, with residents being allowed to return to their homes last night. All five suspects have been detained, and government officials have declined to officially attribute motive.
-----END TEARLINE-----
Analyst Comments: As this is a developing situation, many of the details as presented to the public either are not clear, or do not make much sense in terms of what attack might have been planned. Right now, the finger is being pointed at Iran for this incident for obvious reasons, however before attribution can be laid on any group or nation, the basic facts of the case must be ironed out. Government officials and media groups are insinuating that this was a Vehicle Borne IED (VBIED) attack that was foiled before it could materialize. Other claims are being made suggesting that this incident is not terrorism...but rather a group of thieves who were trying to steal diesel from the farm that they were discovered at. Examining the Most Deadly theory first, if it was a VBIED attack, it would be one of the most unorthodox VBIED attacks in history, for many different reasons.

First of all, multiple people being located in each vehicle is odd; these types of attacks almost never result in multiple attackers being located in the same vehicle...it's almost always just one person inside the VBIED. If multiple people are to take part in an attack, it would have made more sense for the additional personnel to travel to the site in separate vehicles, to conduct a more complex attack (such as the infamous Bataclan attack back in 2015). In this case however, local authorities have not stated whether or not any small arms were found inside the vehicles, and no ideological material (such as flags, banners, or other paraphernalia) was found either.

Additionally, the local farmer who claims to have been the original source for visually observing these individuals stated that she initially became suspicious after these men were seen wearing hoods and masks. If this observation is true (and it probably is), this is another detail that does not make sense. VBIED attacks are usually a one-way trip, and therefore the attackers aren't normally concerned with keeping their identity a secret. On the contrary, they usually want to be known publicly as martyrs, so wearing masks goes against nearly all other similar attacks.

Furthermore, the attackers were spotted by the farmer blocking the roadway, and fled from the scene on foot after the farmer drove up on them. This is once again another clue that something is amiss. Normally, once a terrorist begins moving into the final stages of their attack and starts maneuvering to the attack site, a series of events is in place that would be difficult to stop. Once they've committed to the attack, violence from authorities is usually the only thing that can stop an attack at that point. Following the narrative as presented, five very physically fit Military Aged Males spent months planning an attack, had obtained three vehicles packed with explosives, had arrived at the attack site, and were preparing the attack...but were shooed away by an unarmed British lady right as they were about to detonate. This framing makes absolutely zero sense unless the story as presented is missing large and very critical details.

Another discrepancy is the exact location of where the vehicles were discovered blocking the road. The farmer who made the discovery found these men and their vehicles at a junction on Horcott Road, a quiet English lane just to the east of the base itself. This road is nowhere near a main entrance to the facility. Speculating a bit (and following the VBIED theory), it is possible that the attackers intended to attack the perimeter fence itself, and not a main gate. Right at the junction where the vehicles were parked is a farm which features a small path that leads somewhat close to the perimeter fence itself. However, based on the satellite imagery (which the attackers surely would have had) this is a rather poor attack site. There is no High-Speed Avenue of Approach, and even if they detonated their cargo right where they were sitting, it's not very likely that any military aircraft at the base would have been damaged (although a LOT of citizens would have been killed). There are several other points where the attackers could have breached the perimeter, including one site that is directly on a main road, easily accessible, and offered absolutely zero resistance to a vehicle ramming through the flimsy fence to drive directly onto the runway itself. If the attackers were dedicated enough to fill three vans with explosives in an attempt to carry out one of the most substantial IED attacks in British history...they would have had to drive past one of the most devastatingly vulnerable parts of the base, to pick a far less effective target. Now that the jig is up and base security is heightened, there is no risk to pointing out this glaring vulnerability, because base security have parked heavy vehicles near all of the gates that are easy to ram through. This indicates that the vulnerabilities along the base perimeter were genuine...and the alleged terrorists did not choose to exploit them for some reason.

Finally, the vehicles themselves provide a major clue which adds helpful context that must be considered in the broader context of what might have happened. At least one of the vans was marked with the logo of "Fuel 2You" a fuel delivery company, which provides fueling services to machinery and industrial sites, for customers who need small fuel deliveries. However, the logo is NOT the same as the company...they misspelled the name. The vans are marked with "Fuel 2YOU", but the actual company is stylized as "FUEL2U" with the letter "U". The logo is also green in the United Kingdom; the red logo that the suspects copied is from an American company.

This small detail alone is the strongest evidence of malign action. Camouflage is an act that, when discovered, betrays intent to conceal something. And in this case, it's fantastic camouflage, because if a terrorist were to be pulled over with barrels full of flammable liquid, there is no better camouflage than to take on the identity of a company that is known for operating mobile gas stations. The problem is that the suspects googled "Fuel 2 You" and got the logo from the American company, instead of the British company that is called "Fuel2U". The actual company released a statement confirming that their company likeness was used by the suspects without their permission, and that these vehicles had no affiliation with their company whatsoever.

As a result of this final detail, the suspects were almost certainly up to no good, but exactly what they were planning is up for debate and will have to be determined later on. The use of camouflage on their vans is a clever trick that would support either the VBIED theory or the diesel theft theory, but adding up all of the details that are known, every factor lines up more with the diesel theft theory than the VBIED theory. Speculating on the diesel theft theory, everything so far makes sense. A band of thieves masquerading as a fuel delivery service company, and using that as cover to steal fuel would be a rather slick criminal operation (that is, if they weren't dumb enough to use the wrong logo). Since the suspects were captured alive, it is certain that some information will be obtained, but for now a lot of guesswork is required both to determine what actually was being planned, and also what future threats might be still on the horizon.

The discrepancies in the other details of the case indicate that this case is not as cut-and-dry as depicted in the media...there is very clearly something that the authorities are not telling the public. This does not necessarily indicate much on it's own; there is certainly enough wiggle room in the official story for everything to technically be true. Maybe the attackers got lost, or had a breakdown, or were not that great at planning. Maybe they weren't trying to conduct an attack at the time of their discovery, and were instead trying to stage IEDs for later on. On the other hand, it's also possible that these individuals were not terrorists, but rather thieves attempting to steal fuel from the farm at which they were caught. As it stands, the possibilities vary widely, and until more details are known we just don't know.

More broadly, this incident is a high profile matter that will have several follow-on effects even if it was just diesel theft. First and foremost, the American B-1B bombers will probably be moved around the base, since news helicopters revealed where they are parked. Fairford is not the only base where American bombers are located, and these assets are rotated around fairly regularly anyway. Random Antiterrorism Measures (RAM) are certain to increase at all British bases where American forces are staged, with this incident highlighting the security vulnerabilities at major military installations throughout Europe. If pro-Palestine activists can break into a military airbase and damage aircraft with paint (as they did last summer at RAF Brize Norton), then legitimate and serious terrorists certainly can do worse.

This latest incident is too close for comfort, and if this was an attack that was indeed imminent (before it was stopped), this would be a miracle that highlights the critical importance of a prepared and observant citizenry. Until we know more details, from a planning perspective it would be wise to treat this as a very serious threat that could have killed a lot of people. Regardless of who was behind it (and for whatever reason) if this was an attack and if it were to be carried out as claimed by initial reports, many lives would have been lost, nearly all of which would have been civilian. And the threat might not be over just yet. The local farmer who made the initial discovery has adamantly assured that she saw more than just the five men who were detained. If this is true and if there are other suspects on the loose, this could present a more persistent threat to the local area until they are found.

The tokenization platforms onboarding TradFi asset managers.

There are now 641 tokenized funds with a combined market cap of $35.6B, up from just $5.2B 2 years ago.

That is nearly 7x growth.

Asset managers focus on portfolio construction and risk-adjusted returns.

Tokenization platforms handle issuance, compliance and onchain infra.

These are becoming two separate businesses.

Three platforms stand out to me:

[1] @Securitize

Securitize has grown its tokenized fund assets from $65.1M in March 2024 to $4.3B today.

BlackRock’s BUIDL represents 64% of that total, followed by:

– Blockchain Capital’s BCAP: 22.2%

– Securitize’s STAC: 8.2%

It also works with Apollo, VanEck, Hamilton Lane and Revitalization Unlimited.

BlackRock manages $15.3T, yet chose a specialist to bring BUIDL onchain instead of building the full infra internally.

I think that decision says a lot about where this market is heading.

[2] @SuperstateInc

Superstate has grown from $108.2M in July 2024 to $982M.

Its current products include:

– Invesco USTB: $801.7M
– Bitwise USCC: $156.2M
– Coinbase CUSHY: $24M

Superstate previously managed USTB and USCC itself.

It has now transferred investment management to Invesco and Bitwise while focusing on FundOS, its tokenization infra.

To me, this is a clear strategic shift from managing assets to providing the operating system for asset managers.

[3] @centrifuge

Centrifuge has grown its tokenized funds from $28.5M in September 2024 to $1.5B.

The structure is more layered:

– Anemoy owns and manages the funds
– Janus Henderson serves as sub-advisor
– Centrifuge provides the tokenization infrastructure

JTRSY accounts for $765.7M, while JAAA holds $721.1M.

The distribution is especially important.

Sky committed $1B to JAAA at launch, while Ethena allocated $200M to it as a reserve asset.

Janus Henderson did not need to build its own onchain platform to access crypto-native capital.

That is the real value these platforms provide.

From a macro and finance perspective, I don’t think tokenization wins simply because an asset exists onchain.

Tokenization platforms remove the technical and operational work required to deliver new utilities to products onchain.

The open question is whether specialist platforms like Securitize, Superstate and Centrifuge outperform vertically integrated models such as J.P. Morgan’s Kinexys.

I am currently more interested in the specialist model.

If asset managers can access onchain investors without building their own infra, more firms can enter the market, launch faster & focus on investment performance.

That could be the next major phase of RWA growth.

Across four sessions, Chainlink will discuss cross-chain collateral mobility with @The_DTCC , what happens when money becomes programmable and intelligent, how AI can interact with critical payment infrastructure, and finally what @SergeyNazarov calls the “trust layer for interoperable global finance.”

There is a clear progression here.
Financial institutions are building their own digital environments. DTCC is building infrastructure for tokenized collateral. Swift has its own blockchain-based shared ledger. Banks are experimenting with tokenized deposits, stablecoins and private ledgers, while public blockchains continue developing alongside them.

That doesn't produce one global blockchain. It produces more networks that need to communicate with each other.

And that is increasingly where Chainlink is positioning itself.

Not as another ledger competing to store the world's assets, but as infrastructure that can bring trusted data into those ledgers, coordinate workflows between institutions, enforce compliance requirements and move information and value across otherwise disconnected networks.

That's why today's discussion with DTCC on cross-chain collateral mobility is particularly important.
Tokenizing collateral is only the beginning. For that collateral to become genuinely useful globally, institutions need to know what it is, who owns it, what it's worth, whether it's eligible, where it currently exists and whether it can safely move into another financial environment.

The interesting question at Sibos is therefore no longer simply whether traditional finance will use blockchain.

And @Chainlink is making a very clear argument that it intends to be the infrastructure connecting them.

Last year, my co-founder and I made a HUGE bet on AI-Native services. 

Claude Code is now our most used interface.

And we’ve been able to uniquely blend software + human expertise.

We call it “AI-Native Services”.

Here’s how it works operationally:

1️⃣ Company OS in git

Our entire company dataset lives in one GitHub repo called Company OS.

What's inside:

• company/ - team, voice guide, design system, industry intel
• wiki/ - SOPs, playbooks, campaign guides
• clients/ - per-client context files
• raw/ - client calls, market research, competitor data
• plugin/ - 26 agents, 23 commands, hooks
• skills/ - 79 Claude skills

Data is constantly flowing in to keep it up-to-date.

2️⃣ Client repos

Every client gets their own private repo.

Same engineering pattern as the Company OS, just personalized to their account.

What's inside:

• Their ICP, voice guide, brand assets
• Historical campaigns and what worked
• Onboarding form data and deep research
• Slack threads, call transcripts, GDrive changes
• API/MCP connections to their revenue stack

Result: every team member has full client + company in every session.

3️⃣ Human interaction layer

We still log into some SaaS UIs, but Claude is slowly taking over.

Across 20 team members, the efficiency gain has been massive.

We try to automate as much of the admin as possible:

• Client onboarding
• Content research and ideation
• Skill tuning from team feedback
• Reply triage + sentiment routing
• Campaign launch pre-flight checks

So AI does the legwork, but humans ship.

So we can spend more time on strategy + creative GTM.

4️⃣ MCP + CLI engine

MCPs + CLIs let Claude act across our stack vs. just advise.

Some of our favorite MCPs/CLIs:

• GitHub - Company OS + client repos
• Findymail - email verification waterfall
• Google Workspace - client docs
• Airtable - automation backend
• InstantlyAI - email campaigns
• Slack - team + client comms
• Apolloio - list + enrichment
• Notion - internal wiki + PJM
• HeyReach - DM sequences

Plus HubSpot, Browserbase, Supabase, Vercel, Figma, Stripe, Pinecone, Clay, Apify, Firecrawl, and more.

We're also migrating a ton of workflows to custom code.

5️⃣ Operationalize

As an AI-native services company, we're constantly optimizing how we work with AI and software.

Built into the system:

• Guardrails: safety hooks gate 94+ risky operations.
• PR-based governance: anyone on the team can propose a new skill, agent, or tweak as a branch.
• Workflows-engineering plugin: 26 agents, 79 skills, 23 commands auto-propagated. Agent swarms split tasks into 5-20 sub-agents.
• Self-improvement loop: n8n syncs tech stack data back into the Company OS. Pinecone stores past content + performance metrics for skills to query. Human corrections feed back in.

The way we operate our company wouldn’t have been possible 12-24 months ago. 

But we’re confident that this is the future of service businesses.
